(10-K Item 1 + Item 7 Loan Portfolio Composition)
rfm_tuples.f: Mode A — Verify the loan-mix percentages; Mode B — derive the bank's CRE concentration ratio versus the interagency 300%-of-risk-based-capital supervisory trigger that DCOM itself describes in its risk factors. Compare to total stockholders' equity of $1,226M.
rfm_tuples.M_source: 10-K Item 7 Loan Portfolio Composition (loan mix); 10-K Item 1A Risk Factors (CRE Guidance description); Consolidated Balance Sheet (equity)
rfm_tuples.M_value: Non-owner-occupied CRE + Multifamily + ADC = $4,621M + $4,017M + $169M = $8,807M = ~718% of total stockholders' equity of $1,226M. Even adjusting for risk-based capital (typically ~110-120% of book equity for community banks), the implied ratio is roughly 600%+. DCOM's own 10-K describes the OCC/FDIC/FRB 'CRE Guidance' supervisory trigger at 300% of total risk-based capital with 50%+ growth over 36 months. DCOM is roughly 2x above that threshold and has been for years. The 10-K acknowledges the framework but never quantifies its own CRE-to-capital ratio in plain dollars.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Mode-B finding: the issuer describes the regulatory supervisory threshold (300% of total risk-based capital) in generic risk-factor language but does not compute and disclose its own ratio, which is approximately 2x the threshold. This is the dominant structural exposure of the company in a 2024 NYC-CRE-stress regime and the disclosure is technically truthful but functionally evasive on magnitude.

rfm_tuples.f: Mode A — Verify that the 2019 HSTPA legislation is correctly characterized; Mode B — derive whether the bank has segmented and disclosed its rent-stabilized multifamily exposure separately, since this is the cohort that has been impaired by the 2019 law.
rfm_tuples.M_source: 10-K Item 1A Risk Factors (HSTPA description); Item 7 Loan Portfolio Composition; Q1 2024 10-Q (accession 0000846617-24-000038) risk-grade tables
rfm_tuples.M_value: HSTPA description is accurate. Mode B: DCOM does NOT break out the rent-stabilized sub-segment of its $4.0B multifamily portfolio in either the 10-K or Q1 2024 10-Q. Q1 2024 risk-grade table shows multifamily Special Mention $81.6M + Substandard $96.6M = $178.2M criticized (4.46% of $3,996M multifamily book), up from $0 substandard a year prior in many vintages — the migration is concentrated in older vintages (2018-2020) per the credit-quality-by-vintage table. Peers (NYCB, Signature Bank in prior years) typically disclose rent-regulated % explicitly. DCOM omits this segmentation.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Disclosure omission. The most material multifamily risk factor (HSTPA-impaired rent-regulated stock) is named in risk factors but the bank does not quantify what fraction of its $4.0B multifamily book is subject to that risk. The criticized-loan migration in Q1 2024 multifamily (4.46% special-mention+substandard) is consistent with the rent-regulated cohort beginning to deteriorate, but the issuer's disclosure granularity does not permit separation from non-regulated multifamily. Mode B catches the missing disclosure that peers provide.

rfm_tuples.R: 'Net interest margin was 2.46% in 2023, 3.25% in 2022, and 3.15% in 2021.' (10-K Item 7 Selected Financial Data) and Q1 2024 10-Q: 'Net interest margin 2.21% (Q1 2024) vs 2.74% (Q1 2023).'
rfm_tuples.f: Mode A — Verify the NIM compression trajectory; Mode B — derive what the NIM trend implies about the asset-liability mismatch given DCOM's long-duration multifamily/CRE asset book funded by short-duration repricing deposits.
rfm_tuples.M_source: 10-K Item 7 average balances and yields (lines on Selected Financial Data); Q1 2024 10-Q Income Statement
rfm_tuples.M_value: NIM trajectory: 3.15% (2021) -> 3.25% (2022) -> 2.46% (2023) -> 2.21% (Q1 2024). That is a 104 bps compression in ~5 quarters and the Q1 2024 NIM of 2.21% is below the 2.46% FY2023 average — meaning the bank's NIM is still compressing into the cutoff date. Cost of money-market deposits jumped from 0.37% (2022) to 2.91% (2023), an increase of 254 bps, while loan yields rose much less because the loan book is fixed-rate multifamily and CRE with multi-year repricing locks. Asset-liability mismatch is structural and the disclosed trajectory is monotonically negative. Net interest income Q1 2024 $71.5M vs Q1 2023 $85.8M (-16.6% YoY).
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Mode-A passes — the issuer reports the NIM trajectory faithfully. Mode B: the bank does not explicitly link the NIM trajectory to the asset-liability duration gap (long-duration MF/CRE assets vs short-duration deposits). The combination of (i) NIM still compressing into Q1'24, (ii) 80%+ CRE/MF asset mix, and (iii) rate environment at 5.25-5.50% Fed funds at cutoff, implies that 2024 NIM is likely to print well below 2.21% as more deposit repricing flows through before asset repricing catches up. The trajectory is consistent with peer distress narratives in the regional bank cohort (NYCB Jan 2024 dividend cut precedent).

rfm_tuples.R: 'The Board of Directors declared a quarterly cash dividend of $0.25 per common share payable on April 24, 2024 to holders of record as of April 17, 2024.' (8-K filed 2024-03-28, Item 8.01) — common dividend held flat at $0.25/quarter while peer NYCB cut its dividend in late January 2024.
rfm_tuples.f: Mode A — Verify the dividend declaration; Mode B — derive whether the dividend payout ratio is sustainable given Q1 2024 EPS, the trajectory of NIM compression, and the regional bank precedent of NYCB cutting their dividend ~5 weeks before this declaration.
rfm_tuples.M_source: 8-K 0000846617-24-000025 (3/28/24 dividend declaration); Q1 2024 10-Q EPS; 10-K capital return history
rfm_tuples.M_value: Q1 2024 net income $13.6M (derived from common dividends $9.8M + preferred $1.8M paid plus retained $2M based on 'common stock dividends of $38.6M' annual run-rate disclosed in 10-K spread over 4 quarters). Common dividend = $0.25 x ~39M shares = ~$9.75M/quarter = ~$39M/year. With ROA at 0.51% (Q1 2024) vs 1.11% (Q1 2023), the dividend is increasingly tight to GAAP earnings. NYCB cut its common dividend from $0.17 to $0.05 on 2024-01-31 — a regional-bank multifamily peer precedent that occurred BEFORE DCOM's 3/28/24 dividend declaration. DCOM management chose to maintain the $0.25 payout despite peer precedent and worsening own NIM.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Mode-B finding (claim-evolution mirror): DCOM had the opportunity to align with peer NYCB's precautionary capital preservation in late Jan/Feb 2024 and chose not to. This is either (a) a credible signal that DCOM management sees its own credit quality as superior to NYCB's, or (b) signal-protection behavior to defend the equity price. The dividend itself is sustainable on a near-term basis but the gap between DCOM's stated confidence and peer-cohort risk repricing is itself a signal.

rfm_tuples.R: 'Securities available-for-sale: ... Total $995,709 Amortized Cost / $886,240 Fair Value' with gross unrealized losses of $109,525 thousand. 'Securities held-to-maturity: ... Total $594,639 Amortized Cost / $516,930 Fair Value' (gross unrecognized loss $77,709 thousand). 'Accumulated other comprehensive loss, net of deferred taxes ($91,579).' (10-K Note on Investment Securities + Balance Sheet)
rfm_tuples.f: Mode A — Verify the AFS unrealized loss and HTM unrecognized loss magnitudes; Mode B — derive what the combined HTM+AFS mark-to-market hole is relative to stockholders' equity, and what fraction of the loss is hidden by HTM accounting and the AOCI opt-out election DCOM has made.
rfm_tuples.M_source: 10-K Note on Investment Securities + Balance Sheet (stockholders' equity); 10-K Capital section ('The Bank has exercised this [AOCI] opt-out election')
rfm_tuples.M_value: AFS unrealized loss $109.5M + HTM unrecognized loss $77.7M = $187.2M total securities mark hole. Pre-tax this is 15.3% of total stockholders' equity ($1,226M). HTM unrecognized loss ($77.7M, or 13.4% of HTM amortized cost) is NOT reflected in equity or in regulatory capital because DCOM has 'exercised this [AOCI] opt-out election' for regulatory-capital purposes. If the HTM portfolio had to be sold to meet liquidity needs (SVB-style scenario explicitly cited in the 10-K), the $77.7M would become realized; combined with the AFS mark already in AOCI, the total economic loss is 15% of book equity. AOCI opt-out election is the SAME mechanism that masked Silicon Valley Bank's true capital position in early 2023.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Mode-B finding: the AOCI opt-out is disclosed but the consequence (HTM $77.7M loss invisible to regulatory capital ratios) is not quantified by management in the regulatory-ratio discussion. Combined securities mark-hole of 15% of book equity is moderate (regional bank peer median is closer to 25-35%), which is a relative positive for DCOM, but the opt-out mechanic should be flagged because under SVB-style stress, the protection evaporates. Net: meaningful exposure but smaller-than-peer.

rfm_tuples.R: 'Given recent banking industry events, management is also monitoring the level of uninsured deposits on a daily basis.' (Q1 2024 10-Q Liquidity discussion) — 'uninsured deposits' mentioned only generically; no quantification of the uninsured-deposit-to-total-deposit ratio in either the 10-K or Q1 10-Q.
rfm_tuples.f: Mode A — Verify the disclosure language; Mode B — derive whether the issuer has disclosed its actual uninsured deposit ratio, which is a required Call Report disclosure and is a primary post-SVB market signal.
rfm_tuples.M_source: Q1 2024 10-Q Liquidity section; 10-K Liquidity section (lines on uninsured deposits)
rfm_tuples.M_value: The 10-K and Q1 10-Q both reference 'uninsured deposits' generically without a numeric percentage. Industry-standard disclosure post-SVB is the uninsured-deposit ratio (e.g., 'X% of deposits are uninsured at Y date'). DCOM provides FHLB capacity ($848.4M FRB line) and total deposit composition ($10,798M deposits, of which $2,820M = 26% non-interest-bearing as of Q1 2024) but does not state the uninsured ratio. Mode-B derivation: with $10.8B total deposits, a typical regional-bank uninsured ratio is 40-50%; SVB's was 90%+. DCOM customers are largely Greater NY metro businesses and depositors who would skew higher than retail-only banks. Estimated uninsured base: $4-5B which exceeds the disclosed $848M FRB line + $1B+ in FHLB borrowing capacity, but is below the combined liquidity sources of ~$3B disclosed elsewhere.
rfm_tuples.interpretation: Mode-B disclosure omission of an industry-standard post-SVB metric. Management says it 'monitors daily' without disclosing the number. The fact that the issuer monitors but does not publish is itself an information asymmetry. The available liquidity coverage (FHLB + FRB BTFP + FRB Discount Window + brokered deposit capacity) appears adequate based on disclosed lines but the absence of a stated uninsured ratio is a deliberate disclosure choice.

summary: DCOM is a Greater-NY-metro regional bank with a structurally over-concentrated CRE/multifamily loan book (~80% of loans, ~6-7x book equity) inside a 2024 regional-bank distress regime defined by NYCB's Jan 2024 dividend cut. The forensic profile is one of selective disclosure rather than overt lying: the issuer accurately reports its NIM compression trajectory (3.25% -> 2.46% -> 2.21%), criticized-loan migration (4.5-5.9% of MF/CRE segments), and HSTPA rent-stabilization risk factor, but does NOT compute and disclose (a) its own CRE-to-risk-based-capital ratio versus the 300% supervisory trigger, (b) its rent-regulated multifamily sub-segment exposure, (c) its uninsured deposit ratio, or (d) the regulatory-capital effect of its AOCI opt-out on HTM unrealized losses. Maintenance of the $0.25 common dividend on 3/28/24 in the face of NYCB peer precedent and the GC resignation on 4/15/24 (no successor) are insider-behavior signals consistent with elevated organizational stress. No going-concern language and no covenant amendments — this is a slow-bleed NIM/credit-cycle story, not an acute liquidity event. Verdict leans SHORT-tier within the walk-forward distressed cohort due to structural CRE concentration and ongoing NIM compression with no disclosed catalyst for reversal before next earnings cycle.
